drug_class: Partial opioid agonist / opioid dependence treatment agent
purpose: Buprenorphine is used to treat opioid use disorder, helping people reduce or stop their dependence on opioids like heroin or prescription painkillers. It is also used to manage moderate to severe chronic pain in certain forms. It helps reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms so you can focus on recovery.
how_it_works: Buprenorphine attaches to the same receptors in your brain that opioids like heroin or morphine attach to, but it only partially activates them. This means it eases cravings and withdrawal symptoms without giving you the same intense high as other opioids. It also has a 'ceiling effect,' meaning taking more of it after a certain point won't increase its effects, which makes it safer than full opioids.
common_side_effects: Nausea, headache, constipation, sweating, trouble sleeping, dizziness, and mouth numbness or pain (especially with the film or tablet placed under the tongue). Some people feel tired or have mild stomach upset when they first start.
warnings: Do not mix buprenorphine with alcohol, sleeping pills, benzodiazepines (like Xanax or Valium), or other opioids — this can cause very dangerous slowed breathing and can be life-threatening. It can cause physical dependence, so never stop it suddenly without talking to your doctor. Keep it locked up and away from children. Tell your doctor if you have liver problems, as this medicine can affect your liver.
typical_dosing: For opioid use disorder, dosing usually starts low (around 2–4 mg) and is adjusted up to a typical range of 8–24 mg per day, taken under the tongue or inside the cheek. For pain patches (Butrans), a patch is changed every 7 days. Your doctor will find the right dose for you — never adjust it on your own.
